1: Practical seven and eight. Univariate exploratory analysis on a large real dataset. We use the Superstore Retail Orders, eight thousand three hundred ninety nine orders by twenty one columns, and we go through full code, results and interpretation.
2: Let us set up the case study. The source is eight thousand three hundred ninety nine real retail order records from a superstore chain, covering office supplies, technology and furniture. There are six numeric features: sales, profit, discount, order quantity, unit price and shipping cost. The categorical features are product category, ship mode, customer segment, region and order priority. Every student understands buying something online, so the dataset is easy to relate to. The goal of this practical is to describe every numeric feature fully, compare distributions, and write down what we learn.
3: Step one: load and inspect. We import pandas, read the C S V file into a data frame with read csv, and print the shape and the data types. The shape gives rows and columns, a fast sanity check on size, and here it prints eight thousand three hundred ninety nine by twenty one. The dtypes show which columns pandas treats as numeric and which as categorical. Always run this first, before any statistics or plots.
4: Step two: check for missing values. The code is df dot isna dot sum. The isna function flags every cell as true or false for missing, and sum adds those flags up for each column, in a single line. Only product base margin shows a real gap, sixty three missing rows, which is point seven five percent. Every column we use in this practical has zero missing values.
5: Step three: full summary statistics in one line each. We make a list of the six numeric column names, then call mean, median, standard deviation, skew and kurtosis on that list. Each line is a single pandas command applied to all six columns at once. There are no loops and no if statements, because pandas broadcasts the statistic across every column automatically. It is the same pattern used in every earlier practical, and it scales to as many columns as you list.
6: Here are the results, with histograms and density curves for all six features. Sales, profit and unit price are all extremely right skewed, with skew of five point three nine, three point six five and fourteen point one three. Order quantity is nearly flat and symmetric, skew minus point zero two, ranging fairly evenly from one to fifty units. Discount is also close to uniform. And profit's median is negative, minus one dollar fifty, despite a positive mean of one eighty one dollars, a strong early hint that many individual orders lose money.
7: Step four: robust statistics, I Q R, coefficient of variation and outlier counts. We compute Q one and Q three with the quantile function at point two five and point seven five, for all six columns in two lines. The I Q R is Q three minus Q one. The coefficient of variation is standard deviation divided by mean, and it lets us compare spread across features with very different units. Then the lower and upper fences are Q one minus one point five I Q R and Q three plus one point five I Q R, and the outlier count is a single boolean comparison across every column.
8: The outlier counts by the one point five I Q R rule, shown with boxplots for all numeric features. Profit flags the most outliers, one thousand seven hundred four orders, twenty point three percent, both unusually large profits and unusually large losses. Sales flags one thousand forty two orders, twelve point four percent, a small number of very large bulk orders. Order quantity and discount flag essentially zero outliers, because both features are naturally bounded and evenly spread, with no extreme tail to catch.
9: Step five: a real business finding. With one line, df of profit less than zero, dot mean, times one hundred, we find what fraction of orders lose money: fifty point eight percent. And the median profit is minus one dollar fifty. Combined with the median from step three, this tells us something the mean alone hides.
10: Interpreting the profit finding. What we found: just over half of all eight thousand three hundred ninety nine orders actually lose money, and the median order profit is minus one dollar fifty. Why the mean hides this: the average profit is a positive one eighty one dollars purely because a smaller number of very large, very profitable orders pull the mean upward. The lesson: this is exactly the mean versus median gap from lectures seven and eight. When they diverge this much, the mean alone is actively misleading about the typical order. And it raises a business question: which product categories or discount levels are driving these losses? Correlation and cross tab analysis in practical nine and ten can answer that. A single univariate check just surfaced a genuine, actionable business problem hiding in plain sight.
11: Step six: comparing distributions across a category. We loop over each product category and overlay its profit density curve with seaborn's kdeplot. This is the one place where a simple loop is clearer than a one liner, because we are drawing multiple curves on the same axes. The pattern, load a subset and plot it, is exactly what lectures seven and eight covered for comparing distributions.
12: The result: profit by product category, shown between minus two thousand and two thousand dollars. All three categories are centred close to zero, with both profitable and loss making orders in every category. Technology shows a visibly wider spread, so both its biggest wins and biggest losses are larger in dollar terms. The average profit confirms this: technology averages four hundred twenty nine dollars per order, versus just sixty eight dollars for furniture. That is a real, meaningful category effect.
13: Step seven: categorical frequencies. The value counts function is the categorical equivalent of describe, a full frequency table in one line. Run it once per categorical column, with no loop needed for three columns. Always check these before any grouping or cross tab analysis, so you know each category's sample size.
14: The results. Office supplies dominates with four thousand six hundred ten orders, fifty four point nine percent, and furniture is the smallest category with seventeen twenty four orders. Regular air is the overwhelming choice of shipping, seventy four point seven percent, and express air is rarest. Corporate is the largest customer segment at thirty six point six percent, and the other three segments are fairly close to each other.
15: A different kind of plot: the pie chart. A pie chart divides a whole into proportional slices, which suits product category, since it has exactly three categories. Office supplies alone makes up well over half of every order placed. A caution: pie charts get hard to read past four or five slices. Region, with eight categories in this dataset, would be a poor fit and is better shown as a bar chart.
16: Recap of practical seven and eight. Six one line pandas commands fully describe all six numeric features, with no loops needed. Sales, profit and unit price are strongly right skewed, while order quantity and discount are close to uniform. Just over half of all orders, fifty point eight percent, lose money, a finding the mean alone completely hides. And comparing distributions across categories, like product category, is how the first real hypotheses start to form, continued in practical nine and ten.
17: Questions? Next up: correlation, heatmaps and cross tabs, in practical nine and ten.
